newsitem.title: UK: Concert faces last hurdle -- U.S. regulators.
newsitem.headline: Concert faces last hurdle -- U.S. regulators.

text.p: U.S. regulatory clearance is the last hurdle facing the creation of Concert, the $20 billion merger between British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp after Brussels blessed the deal on Wednesday.

Approval by the U.S. Federal Communications Commission and the U.S. Department of Justice is expected by autumn -- but it hinges on whether the British telecoms market is deemed to be as open to U.S. carriers as America is to British ones.
Here is a summary of the telecoms market conditions and an overview of the development of competition in each country.
REGULATORY OVERVIEW -- THE UNITED KINGDON
Regulatory Milestones:
*1981 -- British Telecommunications is split from the Post Office. Competition is introduced in the telecoms equipment market.
*1984 -- The UK Government offers 50.2 percent of BT shares for public trading and abolishes the company's status as the country's
exclusive telecoms operator, opening the telecoms services market to competition for the first time.
*1985 -- Two mobile phone operators are established: Cellnet, 60 percent owned by BT, and Vodafone.
*1986 -- Mercury, now Cable and Wireless Plc, launches the first competing switched phone service in the UK using its own digital network.
*1991 -- British Telecom changes trading name to BT
*1991 -- British Government ends the BT/Mercury duopoly; establishes a policy enabling an unlimited number of carriers to apply for local and domestic long distance licences.
*1996 -- Britain lifts the last restriction on facilities, awarding 45 international licences, including 21 to U.S.-based firms.
REGULATORY OVERVIEW -- THE UNITED STATES
Regulatory Milestones:
*1971 -- MCI becomes the first company authorised by the FCC to compete against AT&T in the domestic long-distance market for business services.
*1974 -- MCI files antitrust suit against AT&T and its 24 operating phone companes, challenging its monopoly control of the U.S. telecoms market.
*1980 -- MCI becomes the first company to compete against AT&T in the residential long-distance market.

*1982 -- The Department of Justice and AT&T agree to consent decree breaking up AT&T, divesting the company of its local regional Bell operating companies and restricting it to the business of long distance and manufacturing.
*1984 -- Seven Regional Bell Operating Companies are created and spun off from AT&T to provide local phone service across the U.S. as monopolies.
*1996 -- The Telecommunications Act is enacted, establishing a framework for allowing long distance, local and other communications providers to enter one another's markets.
